title: Hardcore FPS immediately becomes Steam top seller as devs list '10 reasons not to buy' it
summary: "If you don't enjoy the beta, just refund it."
body: You know a developer is confident in the game it's making when it's willing to list all of the reasons you might not want to buy it. That's the thrust of the latest dev log for Wardogs , the tactical milsim FPS coming to early access in September. Wardogs has built up a lot of buzz this year, joining Steam's top-wishlisted games and rising ever since. Now it's up for pre-order, and it's immediately become Steam's top-selling premium game. I played a handful of hours in a closed playtest this past weekend and it totally won me over —this thing might be special. But developer Bulkhead also knows Wardogs won't be for everyone—which is, coincidentally, one of the "10 reasons NOT to buy" Wardogs , according to the studio. The whole thing is worth a watch, but here's a few of the more interesting bullet points with a relevant quote from the devs: Early access content: "Wardogs has a content problem… After launch into early access, we'll be focusing on bug fixes, feedback, and a new map… Players should not expect regular content drops [throughout early access]... We want to make sure your expectations are set here before your purchase." The price: "Right now, you can preorder Wardogs for…

title: Believe the hype for Wardogs, possibly the next great multiplayer FPS
summary: A 100-player milsim that's inspired by Arma but plays like Battlefield.
body: I'm seated on the edge of a transport helicopter, legs dangling in the breeze, when our pilot flips on the radio to Flight of the Valkyries. "Duh duh duh duh, duh, duh duh duh duh, duh" three passengers sing in non-unison, their VOIP lagging two seconds behind the actual song. The pilot interrupts the performance with an announcement: "Jump quick once you see grass, because we're headed to the hot zone. How many of you bought a parachute?" The chopper goes silent. "Well then." I realize this is the same pilot who taxied me to the frontline at the very beginning of the match over 40 minutes ago. He's been doing this the whole time, has zero kills, and according to his top five position on the scoreboard, has made over $35,000 of in-game currency. Bullets immediately start whizzing past the chopper as we reach the middle of the gigantic map. Our pilot descends toward an LZ with a practiced corkscrew maneuver that, from the inside, could've been mistaken for crashing. But we land with zero casualties. I touch grass, tip the pilot $25, then get shot in the head about six seconds later. I lay there, bullet in brain, weighing my options: give up and lose the $2,600 I spent on this loado…

title: In a fascinating use of free will, Old School RuneScape player spent 4,304 hours catching 275,196 shrimp and 257,064 anchovies to max out his fishing skill in the worst way possible
summary: "This is getting entirely too much attention."
body: Across the ages, theorists and theologians have wrestled with an irreconcilable question: Is free will an inherent capacity of the human soul, or a misapprehension of things predetermined and divine? Is it a unique function of the human animal, or an illusory quirk of cognition bound by circumstance and necessity? If free will is indeed a figment of our moral imagination, how then do we account for the rare and heroic few who—by wielding their own agency—ascend to heights that shame those of us left toiling in mundanity and mediocrity? How do we answer for the likes of Old School RuneScape player Bosby, who this week entered the annals of history after successfully maxing out his fishing skill using the least efficient possible method in a grind that took over two years? After 2 years and 3 months, I reached level 99 fishing catching only shrimp and anchovies. from r/2007scape Bosby first reported his achievement three days ago on the /r/2007scape subreddit . There, he presented a screenshot of the moment when, after 27 months of grinding skill experience, his account OnlyShrimp99 attained level 99 in the fishing skill by exclusively fishing at the lowest-level, least-rewarding fi…

title: 3 months after the release of Directive 8020, Supermassive Games is laying off even more people
summary: This will be the third round of layoffs in less than three years.
body: Three months after the release of Directive 8020 , Supermassive Games is laying off employees. In a brief message posted on X , the studio said it has begun a redundancy process that will see up to 75 of its people put out of work. "This is a necessary step to help ensure the sustainability of the company," Supermassive said. (Image credit: Supermassive Games (Twitter)) The layoffs come in the wake of a mixed response to Directive 8020 (although PC Gamer's Elie Gould thoroughly enjoyed it, calling the game "one giant leap for sci-fi body horror" in their 85% review ), but that reception feels almost irrelevant. This is the third round of layoffs at Supermassive in less than three years, the previous rounds of cuts in 2024 and 2025 also citing the catastrophic state of the games industry and urgent need to do something —which invariably works out to putting people out of work—in response. That's no lie. The videogame industry is in upheaval, and thousands of developers are being let go every year , seemingly irrespective of the success of their work; veteran Brenda Romero said earlier this year that "we were there in the '80s for the crash, and this is definitely crashier ." That s…

title: Yet another sign the Steam Frame is approaching launch—maybe really for real this time?—as the SteamOS beta adds 'preliminary support' for its wireless adapter
summary: Valve really likes to keep up the anticipation, doesn't it?
body: Another week, another hint that the Steam Frame might be close to launch, though this time the hint comes not from leaks and rumours but directly from Valve. According to recent official update notes , SteamOS Beta and Preview channels are to receive "preliminary support for the Steam Frame Wireless Adapter." The Steam Frame is Valve's upcoming standalone VR headset, and based on what we've seen of it—my colleague Jacob Ridley having tried it last year at Valve HQ —it's definitely worth looking out for if you've a penchant for VR. Though the global memory shortage is of course a looming threat for the LPDDR5-laden device. We'd previously seen a bunch of things that indicate an approaching launch date. Valve itself had previously indicated a launch of summer 2026, and over the past couple of months we've seen signs of Steam Frame imports , a 'Great on Frame' Steam classification , and the public availability of Frame-relevant software on Steam . All this has had prospective Frame owners chomping at the proverbial bit for a bite of the upcoming VR headset. So much so that the Steam Frame subreddit recently seemed to lose its collective mind in anticipation, even sharing hopeful pota…

title: MMO heads rejoice, Razer is bringing out the Naga V3 Pro with upgraded switches, loads of customizability and a ridiculous DPI
summary: It's like the V2 Pro, but a little lighter and a bit better.
body: MMO gaming mice look a bit funky. You probably knew that already. With sometimes dozens of buttons for all the different controls, they're niche by nature. Yet the newly unveiled Razer Naga V3 Pro looks to get around that, claiming to be both easy to use and button-heavy at the same time. In a sense, it seems like a pretty safe upgrade from the Naga V2 Pro from back in 2022. Like that model, it ships with three swappable plates by your thumb. The standard layout has a dozen buttons, but you can replace them with a mere six (or just two) for ease of use. With two further buttons besides the left click, and two more under the scroll wheel, the Naga V3 Pro can have 23, 17 or 13 buttons total. Razer says these plates snap into place in seconds without any tools. The idea being you can flip between them when you load up different games. It envisions players using the dozen buttons for MMOs, six buttons for MOBA and battle royales, then the two buttons for FPS games or everyday use. Head of PC gaming at Razer, Barrie Ooi, says, “The Naga has led multi-button gaming for 17 years, and the V3 Pro is our answer to a community that wanted one mouse to adapt to every genre they play.” Where i…

title: Thief designer says that the immersive sim audience is too small for AAA games: 'There's quite a few of us who think the way to do it is be III or AA'
summary: Immersive sims should get out of the AAA arms race.
body: Randy Smith Evergreen knows his immersive sims. As a designer on Thief: The Dark Project, he was there in the early days of the genre, and his credits include System Shock 2 and Dark Messiah: Might and Magic, as well as Thief 2 and Thief: Deadly Shadows. And he's pretty sure the genre is a bad fit for the AAA arms race. "Myself and other folks who have worked extensively on immersive sims have a belief that the immersive sims that are being created today and are slated for the future are, by and large, thinking of themselves as [existing] in an arms race to be bigger and better," he tells us. And this has been happening for a while. Just think about how Deus Ex: Mankind Divided pushed things in terms of fidelity. Or how big and expensive Arkane's modern offerings have been. They aren't competing with other immersive sims, they're competing with blockbuster shooters and vast open-world games from the biggest studios out there. "Like, you just have to put more money into them, make a bigger and bigger immersive sim. It's got to be AAA, and it's got to sit right alongside Ghost of Tsushima and GTA 6, and it's got to be a game that's big enough to capture the public's attention. But I…

title: Pulsar Feinmann F01 Noctua Edition review
summary: Breezy and comfortable, but I'm not a fan of its price and battery.
body: Would you believe me if I told you the Pulsar Feinmann F01 Noctua Edition is actually the second gaming mouse with a fan I've tried? Back in 2021, I had the unique experience of getting my clammy mitts on the Marsback Zephyr Pro, and I was… a fan. But I can comfortably say that Pulsar's Feinmann F01 Noctua Edition is the most luxurious gaming mouse with a fan I've tried—a prestigious award, I know. It's loaded with great specs, like a Pulsar XS-2 sensor with up to 42,000 DPI and up to an 8,000 Hz polling rate. As such, it's not just a gaming mouse with a fan; it's a full-on competitive device. I suspect the most 'love it or hate it' aspect of Pulsar and Noctua's Frankenstein gaming mouse won't actually have anything to do with the aforementioned fan but will instead be its honeycomb shell. In order for the fan to actually blow cold air on your palm, it needs room to do so, and the spaces in the shell are plenty. They also come with the added benefit of taking some weight off, which is needed because the F01 Noctua Edition is pretty heavy at 73 g. title: Star Wars Zero Company is a very safe XCOM descendant, but its most interesting parts are found in its Midnight Suns DNA
summary: Welcome to the comfort zone.
body: Star Wars Zero Company is giving the people what they want. And that is: more XCOM. The turn-based shootouts, perishable soldiers and those beautiful moments where you survive by the skin of your teeth because of judicious use of overwatch—it all unapologetically calls to mind the two games that have defined the modern tactics genre. It's what we've been waiting for. I've played through 18 cycles of a preview build, and there were moments where it felt like I was checking out a Star Wars-themed XCOM 2 mod, but with huge production values. It is, at times, incredibly familiar. Which isn't surprising, of course. Developer Bit Reactor was founded by Greg Foertsch, former Firaxis art director, and a bunch of Firaxis veterans followed him to this new venture. Risky business (Image credit: Electronic Arts) But inviting comparisons with XCOM, especially XCOM 2, is risky. Look at what happened to XCOM: Chimera Squad. It was a genuinely compelling twist on XCOM 2, but the ways in which it wasn't quite as good as its predecessor were massively amplified by its association. After dabbling in Zero Company's early game, I can't help but wonder if this is happening again. It is very XCOM, but i…

title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer's singleplayer is a clever roguelike gauntlet I could easily sink hours into
summary: Descenders, is that you, my beloved?
body: I recently had a chance to play a healthy chunk of the upcoming Star Wars: Galactic Racer, a—you guessed it—racing game where you can hop behind the seat of a handful of different vehicles: Landspeeders, a skim speeder, and speeder-bikes. There's also, naturally, podracing. Each of these vehicles handles differently—landspeeders are the most consistent (they're basically just a car) and drift well, skim speeders are similar to land speeders, except they have a "knife's edge" mode that lets them tilt sideways to narrow their profile and dodge obstacles, and speeder-bikes are quicker with less control in the turns and, owing to being bikes, are more fragile. I don't know the specifics of how podracers are tuned compared to landspeeders—but based on my experience, they're capable of both agile turns and breakneck speed, and you'll usually only be racing them against each other in specific arcade modes or multiplayer, though they do apparently pop up in the singleplayer campaign down the road. I can't yet speak to the multiplayer, but I can talk about the game's singleplayer campaign, which has pleasantly surprised me in that hey, it's a roguelike, and I like those! Now, to those of y…

title: Big Walk has sold 1 million copies, making it a bigger hit than Untitled Goose Game
summary: The co-op only open world puzzler is a hit.
body: Big Walk has sold 1 million copies since launching a week ago, its publisher has announced . That's a huge figure for Australian studio House House, whose previous breakthrough hit Untitled Goose Game took three months to reach that milestone. It's also pretty huge when you consider that Big Walk is currently a monthly "free" PlayStation Plus game, meaning a lot of people on that platform won't need to buy a copy. Big Walk is also available on Nintendo Switch 2. How does Big Walk's success compare to other breakthrough indies of 2026? Meccha Chameleon sold a million copies in four days and is a PC exclusive. Mewgenics sold a million copies in eight days, and is also a PC exclusive. It took 11 days for Mina the Hollower to sell 500,000 copies across all major platforms. So it's pretty big, but not as big as something as obscenely big as Meccha Chameleon. I'm not shocked that it's sold so well—reviews have been unanimously positive—but it's a sign of the times that a co-op-only game with no matchmaking has done as well as it has. Big Walk may not be friendslop , but it arrives at a time when free-ranging co-operative games are very much the rage. "Big Walk is so chill that little di…

title: Fans spent 3 years secretly crafting a full Metroid Prime 2D demake, and it rocks
summary: Metroid Prime Origins takes the first 3D game in the series back in time.
body: August 6th, 2026 was the 40th anniversary of Metroid, one of the few videogames in history to be so influential it has a whole genre named (at least partially) after it. You'd be forgiven for not realizing last Thursday was such a significant date because Nintendo seemingly forgot itself—and not for the first time . But the anniversary didn't go completely uncelebrated. Posted to the Metroid subreddit last Thursday, a new fan game called Metroid Prime Origins marked the occasion with a "a fully complete adaptation of Metroid Prime for the GameCube in 2D, complimented by a fake-bit aesthetic." I've played the first hour or so, and it's an extremely polished, great-feeling Metroid game that could pass as the real deal if Nintendo ever actually made throwbacks this cool. That "fake-bit aesthetic" means Metroid Prime Origins is stylistically reminiscent of the original, 8-bit NES game, but significantly more detailed. It's not holding itself to the harsh color palette or memory constraints of that console, but still deliberately a bit more "retro" than Super Metroid. For a moment I found that disappointing—Super Metroid is still a fantastic looking game—but the more I reflected on it,…

title: Halloween: The Game is banned in Australia because incentivized drug use is bad but incentivized ultra-violence isn't
summary: Priorities, priorities.
body: Halloween: The Game is the next multiplayer horror game from Illfonic, the studio behind Friday the 13th and Predator Hunting Grounds. Like Friday the 13th it's an asymmetrical affair: one player takes the form of psychotic masked serial killer Michael Myers, while everyone else plays the hapless survivors. It's set to release on September 9, but when it does, players based in Australia won't be able to buy it. Illfonic confirmed as much yesterday via its Halloween: The Game X account . "Despite every effort on our part, the Australian Classifications Board has denied Halloween: The Game a rating," it wrote. "The denial was not based on the presence of the iconic slasher, Michael Myers, or the outstanding kills that can be performed in the game, but rather the presence of a controlled substance. Unfortunately, to our disappointment (and certainly yours) this means that we cannot sell the physical or digital product in both Australia and New Zealand." Games with the presence of a controlled substance are allowed in Australia, but it depends how they're depicted. If the use of those substances is incentivized, that's a big no-no. title: The vibey offroading game with more than a million Steam wishlists has a release date
summary: Over the Hill looks set to be a low key hit.
body: Among the heavy hitters and viral sensations that make up Steam's most-wishlisted games, Over the Hill exudes "little engine that could" energy. It's a chill, vibey offroad driving game that puts you in an old school 4x4 and sets you off among some low-poly hills to get lost. You've got a grappling hook and the option to drive in a co-op pack with a few friends, which may be the key ingredient that's seen Over the Hill build up such a strong pre-release following. It's accrued more than a million wishlists in the couple years since it was announced, and all those folks are about to be very happy. Over the Hill is out in just a couple months, developer Funselektor announced today. October 14th, to be exact, is when the co-op driving game is venturing out on Steam. Console releases won't arrive until next year. PC Gamer's Andy Chalk played a bit of the game earlier this year and came away very pleased with how it captured "the broader experience of being 'out there,' going slow, taking your time, and thinking about how you're going to get where you want rather than just hammering on it. You can hammer on it if you want, and it'll carry you for a while, and also likely put you over o…

title: Overwatch's old battle passes are finally coming back permanently starting next month, but some of the rewards will be left out
summary: After years, Blizzard is loosening up on the battle pass FOMO.
body: Overwatch's next season will finally move the hero shooter more in line with the other live service games that don't purely rely on FOMO for their battle passes. In season 4, Blizzard will "unvault" an old battle pass and make it available again. The details on how exactly the system will work are slim at the moment, but it sounds like a specific old battle pass will become available halfway through every season going forward. It will be on sale for anyone who doesn't own it or simply made available for anyone who paid for it previously, and it will be permanent from that point on. There is one catch however: The premium currency, player titles, and Mythic-level skins that were in old battle passes won't be available in the new unvaulted versions. Overwatch used to have new heroes locked behind a tier in the old battle passes too, but I am guessing they've been replaced with a generic reward. Blizzard says there will be more information about exactly how these will work closer to the halfway point of the season, which will be sometime next month. Ditching some of the FOMO involved with battle passes is always a welcome change in my book. It's a little sad that it won't be every ba…

title: Payday has come to Fortnite, because today's cool gamers are 'discovering legendary IPs in entirely new ways'
summary: The new game is called, literally and in totality, Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience.
body: The ongoing effort to come up with a new Payday game that people actually want to play continued today with the announcement of Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience, a UEFN game that's available exclusively in (you guessed it) Fortnite. Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience "reimagines elements of Payday as a progressive roguelike shooter," with three separate heists—the Jewelry Store, the Bank, and the Harbor—each of them made up of multiple unique rooms "ensuring endless replayability." "We recognize that today's audiences are discovering legendary IPs in entirely new ways," Starbreeze chief growth officer Matt Dixon said. "Integrating Payday into the Fortnite ecosystem through UEFN is a cornerstone of our strategy to engage new players and welcome them into the broader Payday platform." That's the sort of utterance that you're only going to hear from an entertainment industry executive, but it does nonetheless get to the heart of Starbreeze's big problem. Payday 2 , which launched in 2013, is still chugging along on Steam, with concurrent player counts that keep it consistently within the platform's 100 most-played games . title: Persona big boss says 'I think we have to do' remakes of the series' most-neglected games
summary: Put away your PSPs, friends.
body: We're up to our necks in Persona. Whichever entry you're keen on, there's something for you. Persona 3? Enjoy the port of Persona 3 Portable, or the Persona 3 remake, or its Episode Aigis DLC. Enjoy Persona 4? Why, that's getting a flashy remake of its own. Or maybe you're a Persona 5 fan? Revel in the veritable mountain of P5-themed stuff that is sprinkled all across videogames like the fallout of a meteor strike. Oh, unless you like Persona 1 and/or 2, of course, in which case please return to your hole and cease speaking. So it goes. Despite being the games most obviously in need of a gloss-up, Persona's PS1-era games have never gotten much love from Atlus and Sega. But maybe that could change? In a recent chat with GamerBraves , Persona series producer Kazuhisa Wada said that—so far as he's concerned—Persona 1 and 2 remakes are damn-near a necessity. "At this point, I can’t say for sure [if Persona 1 and 2 remakes will happen]," said Wada, but added that "personally, I think it’s something we should definitely do. I think we have to do it." title: The Steam Machine design makes for a frightfully good tissue box, and now you can 3D print your own

body: Achoo! Sorry, my hayfever's been playing up again. The Steam Machine Style Tissue Box Cover (or 'Enclosure') is, practically speaking, just a tissue box. But I'll be damned if I'm not tempted to buy a 3D printer just to make one. It looks very much like a real Steam Machine, sans all the actual gubbins that makes it, well, the real thing . You can download the 3D files from MakerWorld and have one of your own. The creator Boyso expands: "Default print profiles are meant to be used with a 0.4 mm nozzle and a smooth build plate. Additional print profiles are provided where it prints on its side for textured build plates." Boyso also explains: "To keep things authentic, I've included two print profiles: 512 GB [or] 2 TB. Just like the real thing... except they're exactly the same. Pick whichever capacity makes you feel faster." Personally, I'd be going for the 2 TB one—you just never know. title: 1666: Amsterdam has the makings of something brilliant but I came away from its preview with a bad feeling as its early access release creeps too close for comfort
summary: I want to play 1666: Amsterdam's final iteration, I just hope it gets that far.
body: I can think of little else cooler than flying above the streets of 17th Century Amsterdam, in the dead of night, on a broom stick, with a black cat. Looking down on the amber glow of the oil-lit streetlamps is my lasting positive memory of 1666: Amsterdam's preview, but I can't say I had the same fondness for it once I got up close and personal with what was on the ground. 1666: Amsterdam is over a decade old now, the brainchild of Patrice Désilets, director and creative lead of Assassin's Creed and co-founder of Panache. He had to fight for the game, suing his former employer Ubisoft for the rights to it. Now, he's working on it at Montreal indie-based studio Panache Digital Games. (Image credit: Panache Digital Games) "We do between 15 to 20 builds a day," Désilets explains. "So it always has to be playable, it's an iterative process at Panache. Progression is more important than perfection." A lot of progression has clearly been made in 1666: Amsterdam, what with its impressive map, interesting story, and smart exploration ideas. Even just during the preview its world felt impossibly big, but the real question is whether all these grand ideas will be polished enough for an earl…

title: The 'world's first' water-cooled Steam Machine is a Frankenstein's monster of neon pink tubing and external hardware
summary: More Franken-machines, please.
body: Although I criticised the Steam Machine for its hefty price tag upon release, part of me hoped the creator community might do something interesting with it. Lo and behold, we now have the first example of a water-cooled version —and I can't help but be impressed. The Not-so-steamy Machine (as I shall call it) is the work of Stefan Warecka , who claim's it's the "world's first" example. They've posted a short video on Reddit summarising some of the build process, which begins with... attacking the Steam Machine's carboard box with an angle grinder. Good lord. Watercooled Steam Machine Build Video from r/PcBuild Despite the "hack first and ask questions later" approach, the end product is a rather beautiful Steam Machine with a fan-cooled radiator strapped to the back, a custom CNC-ed water block, and lots of external tubing—which is then duly filled with a neon-pink liquid solution. title: Square Enix's 88% profit-bump financial report gives me hope for FF14, suggesting the MMO's finally not having to carry the company for once
summary: Things are looking up.
body: Given the current state of the industry elsewhere— it's, uh, dire —I'm pleased to report that Square Enix, creator of the Final Fantasy series among other games, is doing pretty alright, all things considered. The news comes as a result of a financial results report, shared here by Gamebiz.jp (and translated by Automaton ). In the fiscal year ending 2027, ol' Square saw a major 88.6% operating profit increase year-on-year, mostly thanks to its videogame business—which itself saw its operating profit increase by 91.8% and its revenue by 51.8%. That's mainly due to Final Fantasy 7: Rebirth, which is finally meeting some expectations , one would surmise. title: Sean Murray still loves playing the 2016 version of No Man's Sky: 'It's a little bit weirder, but it's got its charm'
summary: "I've got a real soft spot for it," says the founder of Hello Games.
body: No Man's Sky has changed an awful lot in the 10 years since its launch. Hello Games' space sandbox has received a few dozen major free updates that have added features like base-building, spaceship construction, multiplayer missions, companions, mechs, and even its own version of the Death Star . Speaking to PC Gamer for No Man's Sky's 10th anniversary, Sean Murray said that despite all those massive changes and added features that have transformed the space sandbox… he still likes the 2016 version of No Man's Sky just fine. "I've gone back to the original, played the game without any updates," Murray said. "And I've got a real soft spot for it, to be honest. It's a more esoteric experience. It's a little bit weirder, but it's got its charm." "The feeling that I have when I play it is, I'm alone and I'm on a planet and I don't know what's over the hill," Murray said. "And I really love that feeling." Which isn't to say the updated No Man's Sky, even with its busy community events and multiplayer hubs, can't feel that way too. title: Marvel Rivals hits the Ozempic, comes back 40 GB lighter
summary: Svelte and superheroic.
body: Incredible news, folks: Marvel Rivals has completely repackaged its assets. No, not those assets . Last Friday, the internet's most erogenous shooter announced that it was slimming down. As part of an "Optimized texture resource compression strategy across all platforms," Marvel Rivals now comes in about 40 GB lighter on PC than it did before. This is part of the game's bevy of season 9.5 tweaks and updates. In a chat with a stationary camera, Marvel Rivals creative director Guangyun Chen said that "our tech wizards have been hard at work forging solutions. In season 9.5, we are implementing a massive texture compression overhaul, without sacrificing a single pixel of visual fidelity." The downside is that, because NetEase is rejigging everything, the actual season 9.5 update itself is meatier than usual. "The initial season 9.5 update will be larger than usual, but the final install size will be much lighter," says Chen. It's always nice when this happens. title: Australians must now prove their age to buy R18+ games on the Xbox store
summary: Microsoft is the first among major games platforms to implement stricter age verification.
body: If you use the Xbox store to buy either Xbox or PC games—and yes, the latter is possible—you may be prompted to verify your age the next time you try to buy an R18+ game. Microsoft confirmed as much via emails sent to users over the weekend, which I received. "Starting August 2026, to comply with Australia regulations, you may need to verify your age before purchasing or accessing apps and games rated 18+ on Microsoft Store and Xbox Store," the email reads. To verify your age with Microsoft you can use email-based verification, a facial age estimation check via "secure selfie", a credit card or a government issued ID which can include a driver's license or passport. Email verification is done via London-based tech company VerifyMy ; Yoti is handling facial age estimation, credit card and ID checks. Age verification software has come under deserved scrutiny this year. In February, security researchers claim to have found that verification provider Persona is not only lax with information security but also does a lot more than simply verify your age . Persona is among the most widely used verification providers, with Roblox, Twitch and VRChat using the software. Discord trialed it o…

title: Steam Week in Review: Games about sorting 1000s of mundane objects onto shelves are the new craze sweeping PC gaming
summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending August 9.
body: Games about cleaning are all the rage. The recent success of House Flipper, Power Wash Simulator and Unpacking demonstrates there's a mainstream-sized appetite among PC gamers for making messy places neat and tidy. But the micro-genre goes back way further than that. The 1982 arcade game Bubbles was about using a bubble to clean a filthy sink. Cosy foundational text Harvest Moon—like its descendant Stardew Valley—has you gradually transforming a forgotten ruin into a quaint and personalised space. Then there's stuff like Chibi-Robo and Katamari Damacy. Not all cleaning games are cosy or sim-oriented. Viscera Cleanup Detail is about cleaning blood 'n' guts and The Gunk is a 3D platformer about eliminating space gunk in order to, I'm not sure, probably save the world. And the recent wave of retail simulators have lots of cleaning and sorting. But the cleaning or tidying game has evolved once again. Its newest manifestation may clock as either a living nightmare or the height of blissful stimulation, depending on your temperament.
